text: # Practical Advice for Junior Computer Science Students – Shahrina Khan ## Introduction As a fourth-year student in my seventh semester of BS Computer Science at UMT Sialkot, younger students frequently ask me how to navigate the degree, which skills to pick up, and how to avoid feeling overwhelmed by the sheer volume of technologies in software engineering and artificial intelligence. Below is honest, practical advice based on what actually worked for me and what mistakes I learned from. --- ## 1. Don't Just Watch Tutorials — Build Small Projects Immediately The biggest trap in learning programming is "tutorial hell" — spending hours watching video playlists without touching your code editor. - When you learn loops, write a CLI text game or a grade calculator. - When you learn basic OOP or data structures, build a student record manager or an inventory tool. - When you learn web development, don't copy a cloned Netflix UI word-for-word; build an app that solves a personal problem, like a recipe manager or a task organizer. Real learning starts the moment your code breaks and you have to read the terminal stack trace yourself. ## 2. Embrace Error Messages and Debugging Many beginners panic when they see red text in their terminal. Remember: - Errors are not a reflection of your intelligence; they are simply the interpreter telling you what condition failed. - Read error messages from the bottom line upwards. Usually, the final 2-3 lines tell you the exact file, line number, and

when they see red text in their terminal. Remember: - Errors are not a reflection of your intelligence; they are simply the interpreter telling you what condition failed. - Read error messages from the bottom line upwards. Usually, the final 2-3 lines tell you the exact file, line number, and error type (e.g., `KeyError`, `TypeError`, `IndentationError`). - Form the habit of placing print statements or attaching a debugger to inspect variable states before and after the failure. ## 3. Master the Fundamentals Before Jumping to Advanced AI Artificial intelligence and Agentic workflows are exciting, but you cannot be an effective AI engineer without solid programming foundations: - Learn **Python** thoroughly: understand list comprehensions, generators, dictionaries, typing, and virtual environments (`venv`). - Learn **Git & GitHub** from semester one. Every assignment and project should be version-controlled with sensible commit messages. - Learn **REST APIs**: understand how HTTP requests (GET, POST, headers, status codes) work before trying to connect LLMs to web frontends. - Understand basic **relational databases**: write raw SQL queries, design primary/foreign keys, and understand indexing before using ORMs or vector databases. ## 4. Explore Full-Stack Development Being able to build end-to-end is a superpower: - Knowing both backend (FastAPI/Python) and frontend (React/Next.js) lets you prototype full working systems independently without waiting on a teammate. - It gives you a complete mental model of data flow: from user input in the browser, through API serialization, database persistence, model inference, and back to UI updates. ## 5. Don't Pretend to Know Everything — Value Honesty - Be clear about what you have built and what you are still exploring. - In interviews, hackathons, and team collaborations, admitting *"I haven't used this specific tool yet, but I understand the underlying concept and can pick it up"* earns much more respect than making up superficial claims. ## 6. Balance Screen Time with Real Life - Coding can be mentally exhausting. Find an offline hobby that lets your mind reset. - For me, cooking and travelling into nature (like visiting the northern areas of Pakistan) provide a healthy creative outlet away from the keyboard. A refreshed mind solves programming bugs twice as fast!

# How I Work: Developer Routine, Setup, & Study Habits – Shahrina Khan ## Developer Setup & Tools My development environment is built around fast, lightweight, and modern developer tooling: - **Operating System:** Linux / Ubuntu environment for native bash tooling, permissions, and containerized workflows. - **Code Editor:** Visual Studio Code with key extensions: - Python & Pylance (strict type checking enabled) - Prettier & ESLint for JavaScript and TypeScript formatting - GitLens for tracking commit history and file diffs - Thunder Client / Postman for testing FastAPI endpoints - **Terminal:** Bash shell with aliases for quick Git commands and Python virtual environment activation. - **Package Management:** `pip` and virtual environments (`.venv`) for Python; `npm` / `pnpm` for Next.js and frontend projects. ## Daily Workflow & Habits ### 1. Breaking Down Big Tasks into Atomic Steps When starting a complex assignment or hackathon project, I never jump straight into writing massive blocks of code. Instead: - I sketch out the user journey and API contract on paper or a digital note. - I build the smallest working prototype (a "tracer bullet" implementation) first. For instance, in an AI project, I build the core retrieval function before writing the web interface. - Once the pipeline works in the terminal or a notebook, I wrap it in clean modules with type annotations and docstrings. ### 2. Git Discipline - I maintain clean branches for distinct features (`feature/retriever`, `feature/gradio-ui`). - I commit frequently with descriptive messages describing *what* changed and *why*. - I

Git Discipline - I maintain clean branches for distinct features (`feature/retriever`, `feature/gradio-ui`). - I commit frequently with descriptive messages describing *what* changed and *why*. - I strictly ensure `.gitignore` excludes virtual environments (`.venv`), `.env` files with secret API tokens, cache files (`__pycache__`), and large binary artifacts. ### 3. Debugging Strategy When an application behaves unexpectedly: 1. **Reproduce the bug reliably:** Find the exact minimal input that triggers the issue. 2. **Inspect the data shape:** Check if the dictionary keys, array shapes, or variable types match what the downstream function expects (a common issue in NLP and RAG pipelines). 3. **Isolate external dependencies:** Test API calls independently using curl or Python scripts to determine whether the issue is local code logic or external API rate limits / downtime. ### 4. Continuous Study & Keeping Up with AI - AI moves fast, so I allocate time each week to read technical release notes, explore GitHub repositories, and review Hugging Face model documentation. - When a new framework emerges (like FastAPI improvements, Next.js releases, or new embedding models), I prefer building a 100-line prototype rather than just reading articles about it.

They let a person record tasks and deadlines, but may not help them notice that their workload is becoming unrealistic until a deadline is close or has already been missed. DeadlineOS is designed around the idea of proactive planning. Its project description calls the problem “schedule density blindness”: a person may have many commitments without a clear picture of how those commitments interact or whether there is enough time to complete them. The aim is to bring tasks, goals, habits, meetings, and deadlines into a coordinated system. Rather than serving only as a list, DeadlineOS is intended to help users understand their workload and identify potential conflicts earlier. ### What the system is intended to do DeadlineOS combines planning features with

classification Verdade is an AI-powered Urdu fake-news detection platform. Its README describes the project as an academic NLP project intended for course demonstration. It accepts Urdu news text and uses a fine-tuned XLM-RoBERTa model to produce a classification and confidence information. The motivation is linguistic access. The project README notes that misinformation circulates through Urdu-language social media, while many existing fact-checking tools focus on English or depend on manual review. Verdade explores how a multilingual transformer can be adapted to a specific language and task. ### How Verdade processes an article The documented prediction flow is: 1. A user pastes Urdu news text into the application. 2. The text is tokenized with the XLM-RoBERTa tokenizer, with a maximum length of 256 tokens. 3. The fine-tuned model performs an inference pass. 4. The system calculates confidence values for the output classes. 5. A post-processing layer can return an uncertain result or apply documented heuristic patterns. 6. The backend returns a structured response, and the frontend displays the result. 7. Prediction history can be stored with an identifier and timestamp. The output includes a prediction, confidence values, verdict text, and a prediction ID. The interface is described as supporting right-to-left Urdu rendering, which matters for presenting Urdu text naturally and legibly. ### Dataset and evaluation The README describes a Combined Urdu News Dataset with 10,421 samples: 3,339 in the fake class and 7,082 in the true class. It documents several evaluation sets, including an in-distribution test set, an external test set, and synthetic samples. The README reports 98% accuracy on the in-distribution set and 96.25% on an external set. It reports 88.75% accuracy on the synthetic set. These are results reported by the project, not a promise that every future prediction will be correct. Model performance depends on the data, the evaluation design, and how closely future articles resemble the examples used during training and testing. The different test sets are important because a single score can give an incomplete picture. An in-distribution test measures performance on held-out examples from a related dataset. An external test can provide evidence about whether a model generalizes to a different source. Synthetic examples can expose behavior on generated or hand-crafted text, though they may not represent the full range of real-world news. ### Handling uncertainty Verdade documents a confidence threshold: when the model’s highest confidence is below 65%, it returns `UNCERTAIN` rather than forcing a real-or-fake label. This is a valuable design choice for a tool dealing with information that could influence what people believe or share. The project also documents heuristic overrides for certain Urdu patterns, including conspiracy framing, miracle-cure claims, and suppression or cover-up language.
